name: Mimestream
tagline: Build a native Mac Gmail client over standards-based APIs with local cache

tiers.name: Individual
tiers.limits: All supported Google accounts; up to 5 devices; sharing with immediate family in the same household.
tiers.notes: $49.99/year; sold directly by Mimestream, not through the App Store.

tiers.name: Group
tiers.limits: 1 seat per user; self-service purchase for up to 50 seats; contact sales above 50 seats.

pricing.freeTierCaps: no free tier; 14-day fully functional trial, no credit card
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; auto-renews; no one-time or lifetime purchase
pricing.hiddenCosts: Sales tax or VAT may apply; promotional prices apply only for the stated promotional term. Group plans with 10+ seats may temporarily exceed the purchased seat count for 30 days, after which enough seats must be bought; monthly payments are non-refundable.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Mimestream, build a native Mac Gmail client over standards-based APIs with local cache. The hard boundary is deep gmail api use, native macos polish, sync reliability, and support, plus mail infrastructure, integrations, and client polish.
coreLoopDIY: Connect an existing Gmail mailbox over standards-based APIs, index messages in a local cache, provide a fast focused native Mac inbox, and send through the account's normal SMTP service.
whatYouLose: deep Gmail API use, native macOS polish, sync reliability, and support
moatNotes: mail infrastructure, integrations, and client polish
ongoingBurden: IMAP quirks, OAuth, MIME, threading, search, attachments, offline sync, notifications, secure storage, and provider changes
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Mimestream because an email client can be rebuilt; operating a trusted mail service with excellent deliverability cannot. The recurring cost buys IMAP quirks, OAuth, MIME, threading, search, attachments, offline sync, notifications, secure storage, and provider changes, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: mailcow
priorArt.desc: Popular open-source mail-server suite that demonstrates the operational complexity of hosted mail.

alternatives.name: Apple Mail
alternatives.desc: The native Mac client with a local cache and first-class Gmail support; it uses Apple's ideas about Gmail, not Mimestream's.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Individual plan and a personal desktop mail client DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Mimestream in an empty repository.
Use Tauri 2, React, TypeScript, SQLite, IMAP, SMTP, and OAuth where available; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: connect an existing Gmail mailbox over standards-based APIs, index messages in a local cache, provide a fast focused native Mac inbox, and send through the account's normal SMTP service.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Support one IMAP and SMTP account with credentials stored only in the OS keychain.
Index headers and message bodies locally with resumable sync and a visible status page.
Implement standards-based threading, folders, labels, archive, snooze, drafts, and search.
Render HTML email in a locked-down sandbox and block remote images by default.
Send multipart messages with attachments and preserve a local copy of every draft.
Add export, local cache reset, account reconnect, diagnostics, and safe logging.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out running a public mail server.
Deliberately leave out shared team inboxes and sales workflows.
Deliberately leave out mobile push services and provider-scale spam filtering.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
